summary: Reviewed the dvpwa (SQLI) aiohttp application: DAOs (sqli/dao/*), views and routes, auth utilities, middlewares, app/service setup, Jinja2 templates, config and DB fixtures. The application is riddled with intentional, reachable vulnerabilities. Most serious is an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create reachable from the public POST /students/ endpoint, compounded by globally disabled HTML autoescaping (stored XSS), disabled CSRF protection, non-HttpOnly session cookies, and unsalted MD5 password hashing. Static assets and templates not relevant to logic were skimmed only.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python string interpolation of the user-supplied name instead of using a parameterized query. The value flows unescaped from an HTTP request into the SQL text. It is reached from views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) on POST /students/, a route that performs no authentication check (sqli/routes.py:14) and whose CSRF protection is disabled (sqli/app.py:27). Any anonymous visitor can POST name=<payload> to inject arbitrary SQL. Because the single quotes are placed by the template, a payload such as x'); DROP TABLE students;-- or a stacked/subquery injection yields full read/write/DDL on the database. This is the clearest representative of injection in the code; all other DAO methods correctly parameterize.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  then  await cur.execute(q). Source: data['name'] in views.students -> Student.create(conn, data['name']).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}); never interpolate request data into SQL text.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: Jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False for all templates. User-controlled, persisted values are then rendered raw into HTML: course.title and course.description and review.review_text (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:14-15,22) and student name (sqli/templates/students.jinja2:16). An attacker submits a review (POST /courses/{id}/review), a course (POST /courses/), or a student name (POST /students/) containing <script>...</script>; it executes in every visitor's browser, including admins. Combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie this allows session theft and admin takeover. Only a couple of templates add an explicit |e filter (e.g. review.jinja2:10), confirming escaping is otherwise absent.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }} rendered unescaped; source Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) from views.review.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','jinja2']) or autoescape=True) and remove reliance on manual |e; only mark genuinely-safe values with |safe.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled application-wide
findings.description: The csrf_middleware is commented out in the middleware list, so none of the state-changing POST endpoints (login at /, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, logout) validate the _csrf_token the templates emit. An attacker can host a page that auto-submits a form to these endpoints and have a logged-in victim (including the superadmin) perform actions such as assigning marks or injecting stored-XSS/SQLi payloads. The tokens are generated (sqli/utils/jinja2.py) and checked only by the disabled middleware (sqli/middlewares.py:26-38), so re-enabling is the fix.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]. The check in middlewares.csrf_middleware (lines 26-38) is never installed.
findings.recommendation: Add csrf_middleware back to the Application middlewares list so POST requests are rejected unless a valid session-bound _csrf_token is supplied.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored-XSS exposure above, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie (document.cookie) and hijack any user's session, including the admin. No Secure flag is set either, allowing interception over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True so the session cookie is inaccessible to JS and only sent over HTTPS.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password). Passwords are stored as unsalted MD5 (see migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 using md5('...')). MD5 is fast and broken: if the database is read (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all password hashes are trivially cracked/looked up in rainbow tables, and identical passwords yield identical hashes. The comparison is also non-constant-time.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(); fixtures store md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), etc.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) via a vetted library (e.g. passlib), and compare with the library's constant-time verifier.

findings.title: aiohttp Application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is created with debug=True. Debug mode enables verbose diagnostics and warnings that can leak internal details and increase resource usage; it should never be enabled in production. Combined with the error middleware that renders exceptions, this can disclose implementation information to attackers.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.
